narrative: The model estimated a 56.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That does not mean failure is certain, but it does mean the system judged failure more likely than passing, so your application was denied. The strongest driver was your third-year class standing: you were in the second decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. This low relative rank was the largest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. The second most influential factor was your undergraduate GPA. At 3.20, it was very close to the accepted-student average of 3.23, and in your case it nudged the prediction toward passing rather than failing. The third most important factor was your first-year class standing: again second decile, compared with an accepted average near the sixth decile, which added pressure toward a failure prediction. Your LSAT score, 35 versus an accepted average of 37.18, and middle family income were not among the top three drivers. To move forward, ask admissions whether you can submit updated transcripts or a reconsideration statement, consider retaking the LSAT, and strengthen your record through additional coursework or academic support. Address the low class-rank pattern directly and apply to programs that review the whole file.
